title: The classroom at Nicopolis
hook: the Discourses are a student's notes of Epictetus teaching young men

segments.voice: Yesterday: fifty-three sections closed, and three kept in the hand. Your line was carry three. Which three did you choose? Day three hundred eighty-eight.

Northwest Greece, around the year one hundred. A city by the sea with a name that means victory city. In a room somewhere in it, an old teacher who was once enslaved is talking to a class of young men, many of them from rich families, some sent all the way from Rome. He teases them. He loses patience with them. He tells them stories about their own vanity until they squirm. And in the room is a student writing down every word he can catch. Today a new part of the path begins. Today: the classroom at Nicopolis.
screen: `A CITY CALLED VICTORY.` → `AN OLD TEACHER, ONCE ENSLAVED.` → `THE CLASSROOM AT NICOPOLIS.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. Epictetus was born in Phrygia, in what is now Turkey, and grew up enslaved in Rome. His owner, Epaphroditus, was a powerful freedman in Nero's court. Epictetus studied philosophy with the Stoic Musonius Rufus, and at some point was freed. Then, around the end of the first century, the emperor Domitian expelled the philosophers from Rome, and Epictetus moved across the sea. Second, the city. Nicopolis, victory city, had been founded by Augustus to mark his naval victory at Actium. Epictetus opened a school there, and it became well enough known that young men traveled to hear him. Third, the notes. One of those students was Arrian, who later became a Roman consul and a historian of Alexander the Great. Arrian wrote down what he heard. In a short letter at the front of the Discourses, he says he didn't compose them like a book. He tried to record his teacher's words as nearly as he could in the very words used, as reminders of his thinking and his frankness. That's why they sound like speech. They're in everyday Greek, full of questions and jokes and rough corners. Four books survive. Ancient writers mention more, now lost. Fourth, what changes for us. The handbook was the summary. The Discourses are the classroom. You'll hear Epictetus interrupt, argue with imaginary students, mock the proud and lose patience with the lazy. It's the difference between reading a recipe and standing in the kitchen. For the next weeks, we're in the kitchen. A real classroom.
screen: `FROM ENSLAVED TO TEACHER.` · `NICOPOLIS: VICTORY CITY.` · `ARRIAN WROTE DOWN THE VERY WORDS.` · `THE HANDBOOK SUMMARIZED; THIS IS THE ROOM.` · then, large: `A REAL CLASSROOM.`

segments.voice: If you have a book nearby, any book that matters to you, open it to one paragraph. If not, recall one section of the handbook you chose yesterday. Read it, or say it, out loud, slowly, the way it might have sounded in a classroom by the sea. Listen to your own voice saying it. Notice what you hear that you missed reading silently. Then rest in the quiet after the words. The bell holds the time.
The classroom at Nicopolis. Epictetus' school in northwest Greece, where Arrian wrote down his teacher's words as nearly as he could. Today's word.
Your line: a real classroom. Read one paragraph aloud today, from any book that matters to you, as if you were in that room. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of the Discourses often read them aloud, since Arrian's notes preserve the rhythm of Epictetus' spoken teaching rather than polished writing.

original.note: Greek: victory city, from nikē, victory, and polis, city; Epictetus' home and school.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old philosophy book.

notes: Biography: born at Hierapolis in Phrygia (c. 50–55 CE); enslaved in Rome, owned by Epaphroditus (freedman and secretary of Nero); studied with Musonius Rufus; freed; Domitian's expulsion of philosophers (c. 89 or 93–95 CE); school at Nicopolis in Epirus. Confirm dates and phrasing.
Nicopolis founded by Octavian/Augustus to commemorate Actium (31 BCE). Confirm.
Arrian of Nicomedia: later consul (c. 130 CE) and historian of Alexander (Anabasis). Confirm.
Arrian's preface: he did not compose the discourses as literature, but tried to write down what he heard in the very words, as memorials of Epictetus' thought and frankness. Paraphrased; confirm.
Four books survive; Photius refers to eight, and Aulus Gellius cites a fifth. 'Ancient writers mention more' stated generally; confirm.
